Our learning path is organised using the mathematical topics covered in **Marc Peter Deisenroth, A. Aldo Faisal and Cheng Soon Ong's *Mathematics for Machine Learning*** (Cambridge University Press, 2020).

It now contains **11 full chapter guides and 68 individual lessons**, as well as an introduction, four subject gateways, original numerical examples and a runnable **single-file Python lab**. Everything is written in English, and formulas come with assumptions, worked calculations and interpretation—not just names of concepts.

::: {.callout-note}
## Source and copyright

The uploaded PDF is a 2024 draft of a book published in 2020. The book's text, diagrams, exercises and examples are **not republished** here. This website is an independent educational treatment of generally known mathematical concepts, using the book as a reading map and citing [the publisher-linked book website](https://mml-book.com/).
:::

## One dataset throughout

Imagine a small delivery service. Each invented order has a route distance in kilometres, a number of items and an observed fulfilment time in minutes.

| Order | Distance (km) | Items | Time (min) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1 | 1 | 7 |
| 2 | 2 | 2 | 12 |
| 3 | 3 | 1 | 11 |
| 4 | 4 | 3 | 18 |
| 5 | 5 | 2 | 17 |
| 6 | 6 | 3 | 22 |

The same table becomes a **matrix** in linear algebra, a collection of **vectors** in geometry, a set of **observations** in probability, and training data in regression. With no time labels, we can study PCA and Gaussian mixtures; with late/on-time labels, we can study SVMs.

For an order with features $\boldsymbol x=(d,n)^\top$:

$$
\hat t=\beta_0+\beta_1d+\beta_2n,\qquad
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}
\sum_{i=1}^{6}(t_i-\hat t_i)^2.
$$

The parameters are learned from observed data. They do not prove a causal law, and this tiny dataset is not suitable for real operational decisions.

## Read by concept

The four original category entry points remain available:

- [Linear Algebra](linear-algebra.qmd) — Vectors, matrices, linear maps and projection.
- [Calculus](calculus.qmd) — Derivatives, gradients, Jacobians and backpropagation.
- [Probability & Statistics](probability.qmd) — Events, distributions, inference and uncertainty.
- [Machine Learning](machine-learning.qmd) — Connect regression, PCA, GMM and SVM.

Also see the [interactive gradient-descent experiment](interactives/gradient-descent.qmd) and [interactive PCA projection](interactives/pca-projection.qmd).

## Run all the demonstrations

The [original Python lab](examples/README.md) uses **Python 3.11+ with no third-party dependencies**:

~~~bash
python3 ai-mathematics/examples/delivery_ml_lab.py all
~~~

Individual modes are `linear`, `geometry`, `calculus`, `probability`, `optimisation`, `regression`, `pca`, `gmm`, and `svm`. A minimal test suite checks the mathematical computations.

## How to learn actively

For each lesson: (1) state its practical problem; (2) define every symbol and assumption; (3) derive the relationship; (4) substitute actual numbers; (5) explain what would invalidate the model; and (6) connect the mathematics to one executable experiment.

A technically useful lesson is one you can **derive and explain**, not just recite.
